paths.name: Delete (or batch) the signature self-verification at the end of seal()
paths.hardware: None — pure control flow. Applies to every core, P and E alike.
paths.algorithms: Ed25519 verify_strict, invoked once per seal(), twice per grant_recipient() and rekey()
paths.claimed_gain: 1.50x on the whole single-record seal path. Measured: seal() = 193.16 us total, of which record.validate() = 64.36 us = 33.3%. Removing it: 128.80 us = 7764 rec/s vs 5173 rec/s (my lab3, /private/tmp/.../scratchpad/lab3). This is the single largest win available anywhere in the codebase, and it costs zero new code.
paths.evidence: crates/blindplane-core/src/lib.rs:386 `record.validate(&policy_for(author.public_key()))?;` runs three lines after `author.sign(&mut record);` at line 385. Same pattern at lib.rs:484 (grant_recipient) and lib.rs:529 (rekey), where validate() is called on entry AND exit, so those paths pay two full verifications. The chain is blindplane-wire/src/lib.rs:293 validate -> :306 validate_structure -> :376 `verify_strict(&self.signer_public_key, &self.signing_bytes(), &signature)`. Measured decomposition: validate 64.36 us, validate_structure 64.31 us, verify_strict alone 64.08 us — i.e. 99.6% of validate() is the signature check; all the shape/canonicality checks together cost 0.28 us and are worth keeping.
paths.feasibility: Trivial. Add `SealedRecord::validate_shape(&policy)` to blindplane-wire that is validate_structure minus the verify_strict call, and have seal() call that. Keep the full validate() on every ingress path (open, open_at_head, decode, relay) where the input is untrusted — that is where it belongs and where it is not redundant. Half a day including tests.
paths.security_cost: There is one real argument for keeping it: fault-injection against deterministic Ed25519 signing can leak the private scalar (RFC 8032 section 8.5 warns about this; see Poddebniak et al., 'Attacking Deterministic Signature Schemes using Fault Attacks', EuroS&P 2018). A verify-after-sign detects a faulted signature before it leaves the process. So do not delete it silently: put it behind a `fault-resistant` cargo feature (default off for the batch path, default on for the single-record path if you prefer), or keep it and batch it as described in the next row. On a client doing bulk sealing, the attacker model that justifies verify-after-sign (physical fault injection) is usually not the one you are defending against; on a hardware token it is.

paths.name: Batch Ed25519 verification
paths.hardware: None — algorithmic. Random-weighted linear combination of the verification equations.
paths.algorithms: Ed25519 verify_strict, on both the seal-side self-check (if kept) and the read/relay side that validates many stored records
paths.claimed_gain: 1.89x per signature at n=64, measured against ed25519-dalek 3.0 verify_batch on this machine: single verify 49.52 us/sig, batch n=4 35.10 (1.41x), n=8 30.40 (1.63x), n=16 27.97 (1.77x), n=32 26.66 (1.86x), n=64 26.25 (1.89x). Saturates around n=32. Our own verify_strict measures 77.36 us/sig on the same 4.2 KiB message, so ours is 1.56x slower than dalek single and 2.95x slower than dalek batch — closing that is worth more than the batching itself.
paths.evidence: ed25519-dalek 3.0 `verify_batch`, measured directly in my lab (/private/tmp/.../scratchpad/lab/src/main.rs section [6]). Algorithm: Bernstein, Duif, Lange, Schwabe, Yang, 'High-speed high-security signatures' (Ed25519 paper), section 5 'Batch verification'; the ~2x asymptote is the expected result because batching replaces N independent double-scalar multiplications with one (N+1)-term multiscalar multiplication via Straus/Pippenger. Our own verify path has a separate, unrelated defect: crates/blindplane-crypto/src/edwards.rs:265 calls `basepoint_odd_multiples()` INSIDE the NAF loop, once per nonzero base-point digit (~51 times per verification). It is a OnceLock (edwards.rs:338) so it is not recomputed, but it copies 8 EdwardsPoints = 8*4*5*8 = 1280 bytes out of the static on every hit. Hoist it out of the loop before doing anything else; that is a one-line change that likely explains most of the 39391/s vs 55473/s verify gap.
paths.feasibility: Two independent pieces. (a) Hoist basepoint_odd_multiples() out of the loop in edwards.rs vartime_double_scalar_mul_basepoint — one line, do it today. (b) Implement verify_batch: needs 128-bit random scalars per signature, a Straus multiscalar multiplication over N+1 points, and access to the OS CSPRNG (already have rand.rs). ~2-3 days. Note it only helps if you actually have N signatures in hand, which you do on the relay/reader side and in seal_batch.
paths.security_cost: Significant and must be documented. (1) Batch verification proves 'all N valid' or 'at least one invalid' with no attribution — on failure you must fall back to individual verification to find the bad one, so a single corrupt record in a batch of 64 costs you 65 verifications. An attacker who can inject one bad record into every batch turns your 1.89x speedup into a 2x slowdown; rate-limit or attribute. (2) Batch verification checks the COFACTORED equation [8]R = [8]([s]B - [k]A). That is strictly weaker than our verify_strict, which is non-cofactored and rejects small-order keys and non-canonical S. A signature accepted by verify_batch may be rejected by verify_strict. If you batch-verify records on ingress you have silently changed your validation semantics and broken the non-malleability property the current code deliberately buys. Mitigation: keep the per-signature canonical-S and small-order-A checks (they are cheap, no scalar mult) and only batch the group equation. (3) The random weights must come from a CSPRNG, not a counter — predictable weights break the soundness of the batch.

paths.name: X25519 public-key generation via the Ed25519 fixed-base comb + birational map
paths.hardware: None new — reuses the existing 64x8 EdwardsPoint basepoint table (already built for Ed25519 signing).
paths.algorithms: X25519 keygen, i.e. StaticSecret::from_bytes/generate, and therefore the ephemeral keypair inside every HPKE encapsulation — one per recipient envelope per record
paths.claimed_gain: 2.53x on that operation, and it removes one of the two Montgomery ladders in every HPKE seal. Measured: Montgomery ladder to u=9 = 32.91 us; my prototype via Edwards comb = 16.45 us (2.00x) even though the prototype pays an EXTRA inversion because EdwardsPoint's coordinates are private and I had to route through compress(). Done properly in projective coordinates the cost is mul_base (9.65 us, measured) + one Fe::invert (3.34 us, measured) + 2 muls = 13.03 us, i.e. 2.53x. Combined with batch inversion (next row) it drops to ~9.7 us = 3.4x. Effect on the record: HPKE seal measures 73.80 us of which 65.8 us is two ladders; replacing one gives HPKE = 47.7 us, and the whole record 193.16 -> 173.3 us.
paths.evidence: RFC 7748 section 4.1 gives the birational map u = (1+y)/(1-y), which in projective Edwards coordinates is u = (Z+Y)/(Z-Y) — one inversion, two adds, one mul. This is exactly what curve25519-dalek does: `EdwardsPoint::to_montgomery()` and `MontgomeryPoint::mul_base_clamped()`, and it is why x25519-dalek's `PublicKey::from(&EphemeralSecret)` is much faster than a ladder. I verified correctness in my lab2 prototype: `assert_eq!(montgomery::public_key(&s), x25519_pubkey_via_edwards(&s))` passes for s = [0x77;32], [0x01;32], [0xfe;32]. Our own code already has everything needed — edwards.rs:216 `mul_base`, the OnceLock comb table at edwards.rs:320, and Fe::invert at field.rs:207.
paths.feasibility: Easy and low-risk. Add `EdwardsPoint::to_montgomery()` to edwards.rs (4 lines, needs access to the private y/z fields, so it must live in-crate) and a `montgomery::public_key_fast()` that does `mul_base(clamped_scalar).to_montgomery()`. Then point `StaticSecret::from_bytes` at it. Keep the ladder version and assert equality in tests across a few thousand random scalars. One day. Caveat: `public_key()` is currently used to derive the public key from a STORED secret too, and the comb table is ~82 KB of static memory built lazily on first use — that is already the case for Ed25519 signing, so no new cost, but it does mean X25519-only no_std users would now pull in the table (gate it on the `std` feature as mul_base already is, falling back to the ladder).
paths.security_cost: None that I can find. The clamping is identical (low 3 bits cleared, so the scalar is a multiple of 8 and the torsion component vanishes; bit 254 set). `select_signed` (edwards.rs:284) already touches every one of the 8 table entries per digit, so the table lookup is constant-time in the digit. Fe::invert is a fixed 254S+11M addition chain with no data-dependent control flow. The one thing to get right: the denominator Z-Y is zero exactly when the point is the identity or has order 2, which clamping makes unreachable for a legitimate secret, but the code should still return a defined value rather than depending on invert(0)=0 by accident — write the test.

paths.name: Montgomery's trick: batch modular inversion across records
paths.hardware: None — algorithmic. N inversions become 1 inversion + 3(N-1) multiplications.
paths.algorithms: Every Fe::invert in the batch path: HPKE ephemeral keygen, HPKE Diffie-Hellman, and Ed25519 compress() — three per record with one recipient, and one more per additional recipient
paths.claimed_gain: Measured on real Fe elements: n=4 naive 16.46 us vs batched 4.43 us (3.72x); n=8 7.10x; n=16 12.99x; n=64 35.07x; n=256 61.46x. At the record level: 3 inversions x 3.34 us = 10.0 us per record, which is 5.2% of the current 193.16 us and 9.2% of the 108.9 us record you get after the two rows above. With a batch of >=16 records it collapses to ~0.2 us/record.
paths.evidence: Montgomery, 'Speeding the Pollard and Elliptic Curve Methods of Factorization', Math. Comp. 48 (1987), section 10.3.1. Implemented and measured in my lab (/private/tmp/.../scratchpad/lab/src/main.rs, `batch_invert`). Inversion share of one X25519 measured at 12.6% (Fe::invert 4.13 us against a 32.87 us DH; the 3.34 us figure is the same routine measured with less black_box overhead in lab2). Our inversions are at crates/blindplane-crypto/src/montgomery.rs:50 (`x2.mul(&z2.invert())`), field.rs:207, and edwards.rs:153 (`let z_inv = self.z.invert();` inside compress).
paths.feasibility: This is the one item that forces an API change, and it is the reason to design a real batch layer rather than bolting parallelism onto the single-record function. You need: `montgomery::x25519_batch(&[(scalar, point)]) -> Vec<[u8;32]>` that runs N ladders, collects the N z2 values, does one batched inversion, then finishes; the same for `EdwardsPoint::compress_batch`. Then `hpke::seal_batch` and finally `seal_batch` restructured into phases (phase 1: all ladders; phase 2: one inversion; phase 3: all AEAD + signing) instead of N independent calls to seal(). That is a real refactor — 1-2 weeks — but it is also the piece that unlocks every other batch optimization, so build the phase structure first and the individual batch primitives can land incrementally.
paths.security_cost: Two hazards, both manageable. (1) A zero input poisons the entire batch: if any z_i is zero, the accumulated product is zero, the single inversion returns zero, and all N results are silently wrong. X25519 already guards this by rejecting an all-zero shared secret (montgomery.rs:104) — that check must be preserved PER ELEMENT and evaluated in constant time after the batch, not used to branch out of the batch early. (2) Montgomery's trick multiplies secret field elements from DIFFERENT records together into a shared accumulator. Every operation is the existing constant-time Fe::mul with no data-dependent branching or indexing, so there is no new timing channel, but it does mean a fault or a memory-safety bug in one record's ladder now corrupts every record in the batch instead of one. That argues for keeping a cheap per-record sanity check (e.g. the existing zero test) rather than trusting the batch wholesale.

paths.name: Replace static equal chunking with a dynamic work queue, and stop assuming 10 equal cores
paths.hardware: CPU-multicore, Apple M4 4 performance + 6 efficiency cores (confirmed: hw.perflevel0.physicalcpu=4, hw.perflevel1.physicalcpu=6)
paths.algorithms: seal_batch, and any future batch open/verify path
paths.claimed_gain: +17.6% measured on identical hardware and identical background load: shipping seal_batch (static chunks) 30861 rec/s vs an atomic-cursor work queue 36297 rec/s. The dynamic queue hits 36297 against a measured perfect-balance ceiling of 4*5173 + 6*2600 = 36292 rec/s, i.e. it captures 100.0% of what the hardware can give; static chunking leaves 15% on the floor. Grain size barely matters (grain 1: 36661, grain 4: 35100, grain 8: 34091 in the 256-record run) because each record is ~193 us — use grain 1.
paths.evidence: Measured thread-count sweep (lab3, 512 records, atomic cursor): 1 thread 5173 rec/s, 2 threads 99.3% efficiency, 3 threads 98.9%, 4 threads 98.6%, then 5 threads 89.5%, 6 threads 81.5%, 10 threads 70.2%, 11+ threads flat. The knee is at EXACTLY 4 threads, which is exactly the P-core count. Marginal throughput per added thread: threads 2-4 add ~5060 rec/s each (P-cores); threads 5-10 add ~2600 rec/s each (E-cores). Measured E/P = 0.503. That single number explains the reported 4.25x: the theoretical ceiling on a 4P+6E machine is not 10x, it is 4 + 6*0.503 = 7.02x relative to one P-core, and static equal chunking then multiplies that by the fraction of the batch the slowest (E-core) worker has to finish alone. The current code at crates/blindplane-core/src/lib.rs:578 computes `chunk_size = items.len().div_ceil(workers)` and hands every worker an equal chunk, so wall time is set by an E-core worker running at half speed while four P-cores sit idle.
paths.feasibility: Straightforward and self-contained. Replace the `items.chunks(chunk_size)` loop at blindplane-core/src/lib.rs:580 with an `AtomicUsize` cursor and `fetch_add(1)`; results go into a pre-sized `Vec<Option<...>>` indexed by the claimed slot, which preserves input order for free and removes the current per-chunk result Vec allocation. About 30 lines, no unsafe, no new dependency. Half a day. Second, smaller item: `std::thread::scope` spawn of 10 threads measures 94.5 us, which is 1.9% of a 256-record batch — worth a persistent pool eventually but do the work queue first, it is 10x the win for a tenth of the complexity.
paths.security_cost: None. Records are already independent (fresh object secret each) and nothing is shared but an atomic counter. One thing to preserve: the current code keeps input order via `results[offset + i]`; the cursor version must keep the same guarantee or callers that correlate results to inputs by index break.

paths.name: QoS class discipline (and the absence of P-core pinning on macOS)
paths.hardware: CPU scheduler — pthread QoS / Grand Central Dispatch
paths.algorithms: All of seal_batch; more importantly, protects against a 2x regression when blindplane is called from inside a background GCD queue
paths.claimed_gain: Not a speedup — a 1.99x regression avoidance. There is NO way to pin a thread to Apple performance cores. `thread_policy_set` with THREAD_AFFINITY_POLICY is documented and accepted on Apple Silicon but is a no-op (Apple explicitly removed affinity-set support for arm64). QoS is a hint upward and a hard constraint downward: QOS_CLASS_BACKGROUND and QOS_CLASS_UTILITY are RESTRICTED to E-cores, while USER_INTERACTIVE only biases toward P-cores. So the actionable rule is negative: never let crypto workers inherit a background QoS.
paths.evidence: Measured directly (lab2). `pthread_set_qos_class_self_np` returns 0 and `qos_class_self()` reflects the requested class for all four classes, so the call works — but the resulting throughput was identical (520.9 / 521.2 / 521.0 / 521.5 M dependent-multiplies/s for USER_INTERACTIVE / USER_INITIATED / UTILITY / BACKGROUND) because this machine is in Low Power Mode, which flattens the P/E frequency gap. I also demonstrated the failure mode accidentally and it is the best evidence here: my persistent-thread-pool prototype tagged workers 4-9 as QOS_CLASS_BACKGROUND, and it measured 27096 rec/s — WORSE than the shipping static-chunk code (30861) and 25% worse than the plain dynamic queue (36297), because those six workers were hard-pinned to E-cores. Apple's own guidance is in 'Energy Efficiency Guide for Mac Apps' / the WWDC 'Modernizing Grand Central Dispatch Usage' session: QoS is the only supported scheduling control, and Utility/Background are E-core-only.
paths.feasibility: Do nothing clever. Spawn `available_parallelism()` workers with NO explicit QoS so they inherit the caller's, and let the dynamic work queue absorb the P/E speed difference — that is what got 100% of the ceiling. Then add one defensive API: a `seal_batch_with_qos()` (or just documentation) that warns callers not to invoke bulk sealing from a `DispatchQueue.global(qos: .background)` or a Swift `Task(priority: .background)`, because QoS is inherited and the whole batch will run at 0.503x. If you ever ship an FFI/Swift binding this is a footgun worth a doc-comment. Optionally call `pthread_set_qos_class_self_np(QOS_CLASS_USER_INITIATED, 0)` on workers to raise an inherited-background QoS back up — that requires an `unsafe extern "C"` block, which conflicts with the crate's `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`, so it would have to live behind the existing `accel` feature or in a separate crate.
paths.security_cost: None directly. One second-order note: scheduling secret-dependent work onto E-cores versus P-cores does not create a timing channel here because none of our code is secret-dependent in its control flow; but if you ever add a variable-time fast path, cross-core migration makes timing measurements noisier for an attacker, not cleaner. Not a defense, just not a new hole.

paths.name: Interleaving 2-8 independent X25519 ladders for instruction-level parallelism
paths.hardware: CPU integer pipeline (Apple M4 has ~4 integer ALUs and 2 multiply units per P-core)
paths.algorithms: X25519 — proposed, and measured as NOT worth doing
paths.claimed_gain: 1.04x-1.08x. This is a DEAD END and the measurement is unambiguous. I implemented an N-way interleaved Montgomery ladder driving N independent ladders from one loop with a batched final inversion. Measured per-operation cost: shipping x25519() 32.93 us; interleaved N=1 33.15 us (0.99x, confirming the rewrite itself is neutral), N=2 31.79 (1.04x), N=3 31.22 (1.05x), N=4 31.05 (1.06x), N=6 30.85 (1.07x), N=8 30.59 (1.08x). It saturates immediately and never gets near the field-level headroom.
paths.evidence: My lab2 (/private/tmp/.../scratchpad/lab2/src/main.rs, `x25519_batch<N>`). The reason it fails is measurable too: I benchmarked Fe::mul and Fe::square with 1..8 INDEPENDENT dependency chains. Fe::mul: 18.18 ns with 1 chain, 11.82 with 2, 11.50 with 3, 11.46 with 4, 11.40 with 8 — so there IS 1.59x of latency-hiding headroom, but it is fully realized at just 2 independent chains. Fe::square: 16.33 / 10.49 / 8.08 / 8.03 ns for 1/2/4/8 chains = 2.03x headroom, saturated at 4 chains. And a single Montgomery ladder step ALREADY contains 4 mutually independent field operations (da = d*a, cb = c*b, aa = a^2, bb = b^2 — see crates/blindplane-crypto/src/montgomery.rs:35-38). The ladder is already consuming that headroom; there is nothing left for a second ladder to hide behind. The published multi-ladder work (curve25519-dalek's 4-way AVX2 backend, Faz-Hernandez/Lopez 'Fast implementation of Curve25519 using AVX2') gets its speedup from actual SIMD lanes with 32-bit limbs, not from ILP.
paths.feasibility: Do not build it. If you ever want real vectorized X25519 on aarch64 you would have to abandon the 5x51-bit u64 representation, because NEON has no 64x64->128 widening multiply (umulh is scalar-only; NEON's widest integer multiply is 32x32->64 via umull/vmull_u32). You would move to a 10x25.5-bit or similar 32-bit-limb representation to use vmull_u32 across 2 lanes — which is exactly the tradeoff that makes the AVX2 backend win on x86 (4 lanes) and lose on NEON (2 lanes, and you pay ~2x more limb operations). SVE2 would change this calculus, but Apple M4 implements SME/SME2 for the AMX-style matrix unit and does NOT expose general-purpose SVE2 to user code, so that door is closed.
paths.security_cost: Not applicable since the recommendation is not to do it. Had it been worth doing, the batched-inversion tail would carry the same zero-element hazard as the Montgomery-trick row.

paths.name: Multi-buffer / N-stream AES and any further bulk-cipher work
paths.hardware: CPU-crypto-ext (ARMv8 AES + PMULL), already in use
paths.algorithms: AES-256-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305 — for THIS workload, measured as irrelevant
paths.claimed_gain: At most 0.9%. The payload AEAD for a 4 KiB record measures 1.83 us out of a 193.16 us record. Even an infinitely fast AEAD gains 0.95% of the record path. Multi-buffer AES (encrypting N independent streams in parallel NEON registers, as in Intel's multi-buffer crypto library) targets exactly the case where you have many small independent buffers and the pipeline is latency-bound on the 4-cycle AESE/AESMC dependency — which is real, but the buffers here are 4 KiB, already long enough to fill the pipeline with a single stream's counter-mode blocks.
paths.evidence: Measured component breakdown (lab, section [4], and lab3): payload AEAD 4 KiB = 1.83 us (0.9%); SHA-256 over 4.2 KiB = 4.30 us (2.2%); one HKDF extract+expand = 1.99 us (1.0%); against HPKE seal 73.80 us (37.6%), Ed25519 sign 40.13 us (20.8%), record.validate 64.36 us (33.3%). The budget closes: 73.80 + 40.13 + 64.36 + 1.83 = 180.1 us of 193.16 us, leaving 13.0 us for HKDF, key commitment, preflight, encoding and allocation. 96% of a sealed record is asymmetric cryptography and hashing over 32-byte operands.
paths.feasibility: Not applicable — the recommendation is to stop optimizing the bulk ciphers for this workload and redirect that effort to the curve layer. Multi-buffer AES only becomes interesting if the product grows a workload of many SMALL payloads (say 64-256 bytes each), where per-call setup and pipeline fill dominate; at that point the right structure is an `aes::seal_many()` that interleaves 4-8 independent GCM streams through the AESE/AESMC pipeline and defers the GHASH reduction, which is the same 8-block pipelining already on the task list. Note that the bulk-cipher benchmarks in the README (AES 5.88 vs ring 8.13 GB/s, ChaCha 0.95 vs ring 2.26) are still worth fixing for the marketing claim and for large-payload users — just do not expect them to move the record rate.
paths.security_cost: None from declining to do it. If multi-buffer AES is built later, the standard hazard applies: N-stream interleaving must not introduce a data-dependent number of rounds or a shared table, and the GHASH aggregation must keep the same constant-time PMULL reduction rather than falling back to a table-driven one for the tail blocks.

paths.name: Runtime dispatch architecture: resolve once, not per call
paths.hardware: All tiers — this is the mechanism that will select among scalar / NEON / crypto-ext / multicore paths
paths.algorithms: All
paths.claimed_gain: Currently negligible (~1-2 ns per AEAD call against a 1830 ns operation), so this is a design-debt item rather than a speedup. Fixing it now costs nothing and prevents the dispatch penalty from becoming real when you add coarse tiers (multicore, GPU) where the wrong choice on a small input is catastrophic rather than free.
paths.evidence: Today's mechanism is `OnceLock<bool>` consulted on every call: crates/blindplane-crypto/src/aes.rs:79-83 (`static AVAILABLE: OnceLock<bool>` wrapping `is_aarch64_feature_detected!("aes") && ...("pmull")`) and src/sha2.rs:422-424 for SHA-2. Each call is an atomic acquire load plus a branch — cheap, but it blocks inlining and constant-folding of the whole cipher body. What real libraries do: OpenSSL resolves CPUID once into a global capability vector (OPENSSL_ia32cap / OPENSSL_armcap_P) read at init and then dispatches through per-algorithm function-pointer tables installed once; ring resolves features once into a `cpu::Features` ZST token that is threaded through the API by value, so the check is proven-done at the type level and the codegen has no branch at all; libsodium calls sodium_init() once and fills a table of function pointers (sodium_runtime_has_neon etc. are then only informational).
paths.feasibility: Two-stage plan. Stage 1 (cheap, now): follow ring's pattern — resolve capabilities once into a small Copy token and store the resolved implementation in the `Suite` value at construction, so `Suite::seal_in_place` dispatches on an already-decided enum rather than re-probing. Stage 2 (when the batch layer lands): make the tier selection input-size-driven and static, not adaptive. The measured thresholds from this work give you the constants: single-record work is 193 us and single-thread; a batch becomes worth spreading across cores at roughly 4 records (4 * 193 us = 772 us of work against 94.5 us of measured thread-spawn cost, or ~0 with a persistent pool); batched inversion becomes worth its bookkeeping at n>=4 (measured 3.72x at n=4). Encode those as `const` thresholds with the measurement in a comment, not as runtime autotuning — autotuning in a crypto library is a reproducibility and side-channel liability.
paths.security_cost: The dispatch decision must never depend on secret data — with input LENGTH as the only selector this is fine as long as callers already accept that length is public (they do; the threat model at blindplane-core/src/lib.rs:17 explicitly concedes ciphertext size to the server). Do not add an adaptive/learning dispatcher: a path chosen from timing history is a path an attacker can influence. Also keep the invariant that every tier produces byte-identical output and every tier is covered by the same test vectors, so a dispatch bug cannot become a silent cryptographic difference — the crate already does this for accel-on vs accel-off, and that discipline must extend to any batch and multicore tier.

paths.name: GPU (Metal) and Neural Engine offload
paths.algorithms: None — assessed and rejected for this workload
paths.claimed_gain: Negative. Do not do this. Included because the brief asks to use 'every compute unit', and the honest answer for two of them is no.
paths.evidence: Three independent disqualifiers, each sufficient. (1) Arithmetic mismatch: 96% of a record is 64x64->128 integer multiply-accumulate over 5-limb field elements (measured: HPKE 37.6% + Ed25519 sign 20.8% + verify 33.3%). Apple GPUs are 32-bit-ALU machines; a 64x64->128 product costs 4 madds plus carry handling, and Metal Shading Language has no 128-bit integer type and no carry flag. You lose 4-8x per multiply before any parallelism. (2) Latency: a Metal compute dispatch round trip is tens of microseconds; a whole record is 193 us. You would be paying a meaningful fraction of the work as dispatch overhead unless batches are enormous. (3) Constant-time execution is not achievable: Metal gives no guarantee about warp divergence, no guarantee that the compiler will not introduce a branch, and the shader compiler is a black box that changes across OS versions — you cannot audit it and you cannot pin it. The ANE is worse: it is a fixed-function int8/fp16 convolution and matrix engine with no integer multiply-accumulate exposed to general code and no public ISA; it cannot express a Montgomery ladder at all. AMX/SME is likewise fp/int8 matrix-oriented and reachable only through Accelerate, with no 64-bit integer widening multiply.
paths.feasibility: Not feasible in Rust on macOS/aarch64 without either an FFI dependency on Metal (which breaks the crate's zero-third-party-dependency claim and its `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`) or a hand-written Objective-C bridge. Both cost the project its single most defensible property. The 10 CPU cores plus the four rows above get you ~2.3x on batch throughput; that is where the effort belongs.
paths.security_cost: Disqualifying, as above: no constant-time guarantee on GPU, key material would live in a shared memory pool readable by other GPU contexts on some macOS versions, and the shader compiler is unauditable. Even if it were fast it would be the wrong thing to ship in a library whose entire pitch is that the code under the security claim is auditable in one crate.

Every absolute number below is roughly 2x lower than your recorded benchmarks, and I found out why: this machine is currently in Low Power Mode (`pmset -g` reports `lowpowermode 1`) with a load average of 7.43 (node at 101% CPU, a process called ./s5 at 98%, fileproviderd at 49%). A dependent-multiply spin loop measured 521 M/s, which back-solves to roughly 2.0 GHz — an M4 P-core should be near 4.4 GHz. My single-thread seal measured 5173 rec/s against your recorded 10233; X25519 32.9 us against your 16.6 us. CORRECTNESS BUG in the in-flight NEON ChaCha20 (task #6).** While benchmarking I built the working tree at the time and its NEON ChaCha20 disagreed with an independent scalar RFC 8439 reference in sparse single bytes past offset ~313 (first 256 bytes were correct). ## Dead ends, stated plainly

- **SVE and SVE2 do not exist on Apple M4.** `hw.optional.arm.FEAT_SVE` and `FEAT_SVE2` are not merely 0 — the sysctl OIDs do not exist at all (`sysctl: unknown oid`). `std::arch::is_aarch64_feature_detected!("sve")` and `("sve2")` both return **false** on this machine. Do not port OpenSSL's `chacha-armv8-sve.pl`; it gates on `ARMV9_SVE2` and would never execute. This also kills the headline XAR-for-ChaCha idea (see path #2's security/feasibility notes).
- **SME/SME2 exist but are useless for this crate.** `FEAT_SME=1`, `FEAT_SME2=1`, `hw.optional.arm.sme_max_svl_b=64` (512-bit streaming vector length). But SME2 is an outer-product/matmul coprocessor with no crypto instructions; entering streaming mode costs a `smstart`/`smstop` pair; and Apple does not advertise `FEAT_SME_FA64`, so most of the A64/NEON instruction set (including AES/PMULL/SHA) is **unavailable while in streaming mode**. Rust's SME detection is also still unstable (`stdarch_aarch64_feature_detection`, rust#127764). Ignore SME entirely.
- **EOR3 does not help ChaCha20.** ChaCha's quarter round contains only 2-way XORs (`d ^= a`). There is no 3-way XOR anywhere in the cipher. I confirmed OpenSSL's `chacha-armv8.pl` uses neither `eor3` nor `xar`, and ring's `chacha20_poly1305_armv8-ios64.S` contains **zero** occurrences of `eor3|xar|bcax|rax1`.

## Constant-time note that applies to everything above

`hw.optional.arm.FEAT_DIT = 1` on M4. Apple documents that on Apple Silicon you should set `PSTATE.DIT` (Data Independent Timing) around secret-dependent code to *guarantee* fixed-latency execution for the DIT-covered instruction set; without it, data-independent timing is a microarchitectural implementation detail, not an architectural guarantee. None of the instructions recommended here (SHA512H/H2/SU0/SU1, EOR3/BCAX/XAR/RAX1, AESE/AESMC, PMULL, REV32, TBL, SRI/SHL) are data-dependent, but if you want a defensible constant-time story on Apple Silicon, setting DIT around the field arithmetic and the AEAD cores is the right move and is currently not done anywhere in the crate.

paths.algorithms: Ed25519 verify_strict (ours 39391/s vs ed25519-dalek 55473/s)
paths.claimed_gain: Closes most of the 1.41x verify gap. Three separable wins: T-free doublings save one field multiplication on each of ~255 doublings per verification; Niels-form tables save 1-2 field multiplications per addition; width-8 NAF for the fixed basepoint cuts basepoint additions from ~43 to ~28. Plus one outright bug fix worth a measurable amount on its own (below).
paths.evidence: curve25519-dalek-4.1.3/src/backend/serial/scalar_mul/vartime_double_base.rs shows exactly what dalek does differently: (1) `a.non_adjacent_form(5)` for the variable point but `b.non_adjacent_form(8)` for the fixed basepoint under `precomputed-tables`; (2) `table_B = &constants::AFFINE_ODD_MULTIPLES_OF_BASEPOINT`, a NafLookupTable8 of AffineNielsPoint (y+x, y-x, 2dxy) — affine-Niels mixed addition is 7M vs 8M projective-Niels vs 9M full extended; (3) `table_A = NafLookupTable5::<ProjectiveNielsPoint>::from(A)` precomputes (Y+X, Y-X, Z, 2dT) once per entry; (4) the loop runs `ProjectivePoint -> CompletedPoint -> ProjectivePoint`, so `r.double()` NEVER computes T. dalek's own docs quantify the basepoint table: radix-16 = 30KB/64 additions, radix-64 = 120KB/43A, radix-128 = 240KB/37A, radix-256 = 480KB/33A. Your head-crypto/src/edwards.rs uses a single EdwardsPoint (X,Y,Z,T) everywhere, so every one of ~255 `acc.double()` calls computes T that the next doubling discards. SEPARATE BUG: edwards.rs:265 calls `basepoint_odd_multiples()` INSIDE the NAF loop; it is OnceLock-memoized but returns `*ODD.get_or_init(...)` BY VALUE — that is a 1280-byte copy (8 points x 4 Fe x [u64;5]) plus an atomic load on every nonzero b_naf digit, ~43 times per verification, ~55 KB of pointless memcpy per verify. Hoist it out of the loop and return a reference.
paths.feasibility: MEDIUM, and entirely in safe Rust — no intrinsics, no unsafe, no CPU feature. Add ProjectiveNielsPoint/AffineNielsPoint/CompletedPoint/ProjectivePoint model types to edwards.rs and route vartime_double_scalar_mul_basepoint through them; add a width-8 NAF and a 64-entry affine-Niels basepoint table. The `basepoint_odd_multiples()` hoist is a two-line fix you can do immediately and independently. For the field layer, your 5x51 limb representation is already the right choice on aarch64 (dalek's u64 serial backend uses the same); Emil Lenngren's aarch64 assembly and lib25519 go further with hand-scheduled UMULH chains, but that is assembly and out of scope given `unsafe_code = forbid`.
paths.security_cost: NONE — and this is important: verify operates only on public data (public key A, signature R and S, message). Variable-time NAF, variable-time table lookups and early-exit are all standard and safe here; dalek does exactly this. Do NOT apply any of these variable-time techniques to `mul_base` or `mul` on secret scalars — those must keep the current constant-time select_signed over the full table. Keep the strict checks (canonical S, small-order rejection) exactly as they are.

paths.name: Metal ChaCha20 / ChaCha20-Poly1305 bulk offload (the ONLY winning regime)
paths.algorithms: ChaCha20, ChaCha20-Poly1305, XChaCha20-Poly1305. Bulk only, never per-record.
paths.claimed_gain: MEASURED ON THIS M4, not cited: full constant-time ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD in Metal = 39.8 GB/s at 4 MiB, 33-34 GB/s at 16-64 MiB, 18.7 GB/s at 1 MiB. Our CPU ChaCha20-Poly1305 = 0.60 GB/s single-thread, 5.66 GB/s across 10 threads. So 6.0x vs our whole CPU, ~2.6x vs a hypothetical ring-quality NEON port (ring is 2.29/0.95 = 2.4x ours, so ~13 GB/s at 10 threads). ChaCha20 alone (no MAC) = 37-63 GB/s. BUT: our CPU AES-256-GCM already does 26.3 GB/s on 10 threads, so if AES-GCM is permitted the GPU ChaCha path is worth ~1.3x at best and is not worth building.
paths.evidence: Primary evidence is my own Metal kernels run on this machine: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-serhiirihgt-dev-blindplane/6578a689-83e9-437d-80fa-e418e95f03b4/scratchpad/bench3.swift (kernel `chacha20poly1305`, real RFC 8439 ChaCha20 + real 5x26-bit-limb Poly1305, 1 KiB per thread) and gpubench.swift (kernel `chacha20_xor`). Literature agrees ChaCha is the GPU-friendly one: AsyncGBP (ICPP 2023, dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3605573.3605620) ships GPU ChaCha20-Poly1305 and reports 672.64 Gbps = 84 GB/s on an RTX 3070; a single-GPU ChaCha20 reaching 211 GB/s is reported in the ISPA 2021 hybrid CPU/GPU paper (cloud-conf.net/ispa2021/proc/pdfs/...264600b171.pdf). Those are discrete GPUs with 10-20x our GPU's silicon and are kernel-only numbers.
paths.feasibility: Genuinely easy, which is the trap. Metal.framework is present with no Xcode (runtime `makeLibrary(source:)` works; the offline `metal` compiler is absent on this box). Unified memory means `MTLResourceStorageModeShared` buffers are zero-copy - I encrypted directly out of a host pointer with no staging. But it breaks the crate's defining property: zero third-party runtime deps becomes a hard dependency on Metal.framework, Objective-C runtime, and a `.metallib`, plus an unsafe FFI surface, plus macOS/iOS-only code that CI cannot run headless on Linux. Precise regime where it wins: contiguous plaintext >= 4 MiB per dispatch, caller tolerates >= 200 us added latency, ChaCha is mandated (AES-GCM disallowed), and the CPU is simultaneously busy with other work.
paths.security_cost: This one is actually clean. ChaCha20 and Poly1305 are pure ARX - no S-boxes, no table lookups, no data-dependent addresses or branches - so the kernel is constant-time by construction on the GPU exactly as it is on the CPU. Real costs are elsewhere: (1) plaintext and the ChaCha key must live in a `MTLBuffer` that the GPU, the Metal driver, and any other process's shader could in principle observe; Metal has no equivalent of mlock/`secure_erase` guarantees and no way to prove the driver did not retain a copy. (2) You cannot zeroize GPU-resident key material with confidence. (3) Apple GPU firmware/driver is a large closed-source addition to the TCB for a crate whose selling point is auditability.

paths.name: Metal bitsliced AES-256 (constant-time AES on GPU)
paths.algorithms: AES-256-CTR / AES-256-GCM cipher core
paths.claimed_gain: LOSES. Measured: bitsliced AES-128 = 30.5 GB/s at 64 MiB, 28.7 GB/s at 16 MiB. AES-256 is 14 rounds not 10, so 30.5 x 10/14 = 21.8 GB/s. Our CPU AES-256-GCM with the GHASH included already does 26.3 GB/s across 10 threads. Decisive framing: even if the MAC were FREE, constant-time GPU AES-256 (21.8 GB/s) is slower than the CPU doing AES-256 *and* GHASH (26.3 GB/s). This conclusion is independent of how good my GHASH kernel is.
paths.evidence: My kernel `aes128_bitsliced` in bench2.swift: Kasper-Schwabe 8-bit-plane layout as 8x uint4 registers, 8 AES blocks (128 B) per thread, Boyar-Peralta 113-gate S-box (top linear transform is the real BP wiring; the 30-AND/53-XOR middle and 26-XOR bottom are gate-count-faithful, so this is a throughput probe, not a correctness-verified AES - if anything it slightly UNDER-counts ShiftRows/MixColumns, making 30.5 GB/s an upper bound). Cross-check: my `aluprobe` kernel measures 1249 Gop/s of 32-bit integer ALU on this GPU; bitsliced AES-128 costs ~57 uint32 ops/byte, predicting 21.9 GB/s - the two independent estimates agree. Literature: Nishikawa et al., 'Implementation of Bitsliced AES Encryption on CUDA-Enabled GPU' (link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-319-64701-2_20) hit 605.9 Gbps = 75.7 GB/s on a Tesla P100, only 8% better than their table-based version; 'Speed Record of AES-CTR and AES-ECB Bit-Sliced Implementation on GPUs' continues this line.
paths.feasibility: Would take days to write and validate a correct bitsliced AES-256 in MSL, and it is dead on arrival. Note the M4 GPU has NO AES instruction - unlike the CPU, which has ARMv8 AESE/AESMC that we already use. That single fact is the whole story: the CPU does an AES round in 1-2 instructions, the GPU needs ~180. Metal does provide the bit-manipulation helpers you would want (`extract_bits`, `insert_bits`, `reverse_bits`, `popcount`, `clz`/`ctz`, native uint4 bitwise ops, SIMD-group shuffles), and register pressure was not the limiter - `maxTotalThreadsPerThreadgroup` stayed at 1024 for the bitsliced kernel. It is simply an instruction-count loss.
paths.security_cost: Bitslicing is the right answer *if* you must do AES on a GPU: it is naturally constant-time (pure boolean ops, no table indices). It is the documented defence against the GPU cache-timing literature. But the key still lives in GPU-visible memory, so the key-exposure and non-zeroizable concerns from the ChaCha row apply unchanged.

paths.name: Metal T-table AES-CTR (the classic GPU-AES approach from the literature)
paths.algorithms: AES-128/256-CTR
paths.claimed_gain: LOSES on speed AND is broken on security. Measured: 14.8 GB/s peak at 1 MiB, 10-13 GB/s at 16-256 MiB, with 4 KiB of T-tables cooperatively staged into threadgroup memory. That is 2x SLOWER than my constant-time bitsliced kernel (30.5 GB/s) - the table lookups serialize on the load/store unit while bitslicing rides the ALU. The entire classical GPU-AES literature is optimizing the wrong thing for this hardware.
paths.evidence: My kernel `aes128ctr_ttab` in gpubench.swift (real AES S-box computed in GF(2^8) on the host, 4x256-word Te tables, 9 full rounds + S-box final round). The historical arc for context: Manavski 2007 = 8.28 Gbps on an 8800GTX; Iwai/Nishikawa ~35 Gbps on a GTX285 ('Acceleration of AES encryption on CUDA GPU', jstage.jst.go.jp/article/ijnc/2/1/2_131/_pdf); GTX 780 78 Gbps, TITAN X 201 Gbps, GTX 1080 277 Gbps; RTX 2070 Super 878.6 Gbps = 110 GB/s (eprint.iacr.org/2021/646.pdf, 'Optimization of AES on GPUs'). Every one of those is a kernel-only number on a discrete GPU.
paths.feasibility: Trivially implementable - I did it in an afternoon - and it should be rejected anyway.
paths.security_cost: DISQUALIFYING. This is exactly the construction broken by Jiang, Fei and Kaeli, 'A complete key recovery timing attack on a GPU', HPCA 2016 (ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/7446081): full 128-bit AES key recovered from a Kepler K40 using 10M timing samples, exploiting SIMT memory coalescing and shared-memory bank conflicts on the T-table indices. Follow-ups: 'A Novel Side-Channel Timing Attack on GPUs' (GLSVLSI 2017, dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3060403.3060462) and 'Trident: A Hybrid Correlation-Collision GPU Cache Timing Attack for AES Key Recovery' (ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/9407157), which recovers all key bytes on modern sectored-cache GPUs. Worse than on CPU: we have no way to inspect or control Apple GPU cache/bank behaviour, and WebGPU-SPY (arxiv.org/pdf/2401.04349) shows GPU cache attacks are reachable even from a browser sandbox. A crate that advertises constant-time execution must not ship this.

paths.name: Metal GHASH / GF(2^128) for AES-GCM without PMULL
paths.algorithms: AES-GCM authentication tag
paths.claimed_gain: LOSES catastrophically - this is the single worst number I measured. Constant-time GHASH on the M4 GPU = 3.86 GB/s. Composed serially with bitsliced AES-256 (21.8 GB/s) that gives full constant-time AES-256-GCM on GPU = 3.2 GB/s, versus 26.3 GB/s on our CPU: the GPU is 8x slower. Robustness check: even if my GHASH kernel were 10x faster (38.6 GB/s), combined AES-256-GCM would be 1/(1/21.8 + 1/38.6) = 13.9 GB/s, still barely half the CPU.
paths.evidence: My kernel `ghash_ct` in bench2.swift: branch-free bit-serial `clmul32` (32 iterations, mask = 0-((b>>i)&1), no data-dependent control flow), schoolbook 16x clmul32 for a 128x128 carryless product, then reduction mod x^128+x^7+x^2+x+1. Root cause is structural: the CPU has ARMv8 PMULL and does a 64x64 carryless multiply in one instruction (we already use it); the M4 GPU has NO carryless-multiply instruction at all, so each one costs ~96 emulated ops. Karatsuba (9 clmuls instead of 16) buys ~1.7x; a GF(2)-linear-map bitsliced GHASH could in principle do better but needs ~128 live registers per thread and would spill hard.
paths.feasibility: The fast GPU GHASH used in the literature is Shoup 4-bit table lookup, which reintroduces exactly the table-timing problem from the row above. There is no good option here.
paths.security_cost: Table-based GHASH leaks the hash subkey H through the same shared-memory bank-conflict channel as T-table AES. My bit-serial version is constant-time but 3.86 GB/s. Note this is also the argument for preferring ChaCha20-Poly1305 on GPU: Poly1305 needs only 32x32 integer multiplies, which the GPU does have (I measured 302.8 G 32-bit multiplies/s), and my Poly1305 kernel hits 75-92 GB/s standalone - 20x faster than GHASH.

paths.name: Kernel-launch latency as a hard floor for per-record sealing
paths.algorithms: All of them, for Blindplane's actual sealed-record workload
paths.claimed_gain: DISQUALIFYING for the primary use case. Measured commit->completion round trip for an EMPTY kernel with one thread: min 101 us, p50 184-287 us, p99 up to 760 us, and it did NOT improve with a hot GPU (a background load kept clocks up; p50 was 287 us hot vs 285 us idle). Breakdown via MTLCommandBuffer timestamps: GPU execution window 2.87 us min / 5.17 us p50 - the GPU itself is fast - but kernelStart->gpuStart is 42.6 us min / 92.8 us p50, and the rest is driver submission plus CPU thread wakeup. CPU-side encode+commit alone is 31 us. Compare: our CPU seals a 4 KiB record in 1.7 us (587,706 records/s single-thread, 5.29M/s across 10 threads). The GPU dispatch floor alone is 70-110x the entire CPU operation.
paths.evidence: Section 1 of gpubench.swift (2000 iterations each) and section D of bench3.swift, which separates gpuStartTime/gpuEndTime/kernelStartTime. Single-dispatch end-to-end for real work confirms it: 1 KiB = 167 us min, 4 KiB = 173 us, 64 KiB = 119 us, 1 MiB = 197 us - i.e. below ~1 MiB the time is pure overhead and effective throughput is 0.02-0.44 GB/s. Note this is 3-20x worse than the '10-50 us Metal dispatch overhead' folklore you find in blog posts; I measured it rather than trusting it.
paths.feasibility: Batching is the only mitigation and it converts a latency problem into a different latency problem. Quantitatively, batching N bytes: t_gpu = 150us + N/34e9 vs t_cpu = N/26.3e9 gives break-even at N = 17.4 MB per dispatch. For 4 KiB sealed records that is ~4,250 records batched per dispatch, which adds >=150 us of latency to every record and destroys the streaming property of the wire format.
paths.security_cost: A batching layer that holds thousands of plaintext records in a GPU-shared buffer waiting for a dispatch is a much larger and longer-lived plaintext exposure window than sealing each record on the CPU and zeroizing immediately.

paths.name: The unified-memory roofline (why the discrete-GPU literature does not transfer)
paths.algorithms: All bulk AEAD
paths.claimed_gain: This is the finding that settles the whole question. Measured DRAM ceiling on this M4: 43.8 GB/s of memcpy at 10 threads = 87.5 GB/s of read+write traffic (1 GiB working set, well past the SLC); the GPU's own streaming kernel independently tops out at 46.9 GB/s processed = ~94 GB/s traffic. In-place AEAD costs exactly 2 bytes of DRAM traffic per byte, so NO compute unit on this machine can exceed ~44-47 GB/s of in-place AEAD, ever. Contention experiment: CPU AES-256-GCM alone on 10 threads = 26.3 GB/s; GPU ChaCha20-Poly1305 alone = 31.1 GB/s; both concurrently = CPU 22.3 + GPU 24.6 = 46.9 GB/s combined. The combined figure IS the roofline. The apparent 1.78x from adding the GPU exists only because Low Power Mode has the CPU clocked down; at full power the CPU alone reaches ~36-44 GB/s and the GPU has almost nothing left to add.
paths.evidence: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-serhiirihgt-dev-blindplane/6578a689-83e9-437d-80fa-e418e95f03b4/scratchpad/rl.c (threaded memcpy, 1 GiB working set, with an asm memory barrier - my first version was silently optimized away and reported 1e9 GB/s, which is why the barrier is there), plus the concurrent CPU/GPU run driven by cpuagg/src/main.rs `contend` mode against bench3.swift `contend` mode. M4 spec bandwidth is 120 GB/s LPDDR5x-7500, so ~88-94 GB/s achieved is 73-78% of peak, which is a believable real-world figure.
paths.feasibility: You asked how unified memory changes the break-even versus the discrete-GPU literature. It changes it in BOTH directions and the second one is the one people miss. Good: there is no PCIe copy, so the transfer cost that dominates every discrete-GPU crypto paper (PCIe Gen4 x16 practical ~25 GB/s, which alone caps a discrete GPU at ~12.5 GB/s for read-in/write-out regardless of how fast the kernel is - this is why SSLShader's 110 GB/s-class kernels delivered only 13 Gbps of real TLS) simply does not exist here. Bad: precisely because memory is unified, the GPU and CPU draw from ONE 120 GB/s memory controller. On a discrete GPU the 500+ GB/s of GDDR is additional bandwidth; on an M4 it is the same bandwidth. GPU offload here does not add a second memory system, it splits the one you already have.
paths.security_cost: None specific - this is an architectural bound, not a security property. It is the reason the honest answer is 'no' regardless of implementation quality.

paths.name: Metal Performance Shaders / any Apple-provided GPU crypto
paths.algorithms: None
paths.claimed_gain: Zero. Apple exposes no crypto primitives on the GPU at all.
paths.evidence: I enumerated the shipped MPS sub-frameworks on this machine: MPSCore, MPSImage, MPSMatrix, MPSNDArray, MPSNeuralNetwork, MPSRayIntersector, MPSFunctions, MPSHost, MPSBenchmarkLoop. There is no crypto framework, and grepping the MacOSX.sdk MPS headers for aes/sha256/cipher/crypt returns only false positives from matrix and NDArray headers. CryptoKit and CommonCrypto are CPU-only and route to the ARMv8 crypto extensions or the Secure Enclave, never to the GPU. paths.security_cost: The absence of any Metal crypto ecosystem means no peer review, no published test vectors for GPU kernels, and no other project finding our bugs. For a crate whose pitch is auditability, being the only user of a hand-rolled GPU AES is a real risk, not a neutral fact.

notes:
VERDICT: the earlier dismissal was right, but for the wrong reason. The usual hand-wave is "PCIe transfer kills it" - that argument is invalid on Apple Silicon, and the user is correct that it was dismissed too fast. Unified memory genuinely removes the transfer cost; I encrypted straight out of host pointers with zero copies. GPU crypto loses here for two different and much stronger reasons: (1) the M4 GPU has no AES instruction and no carryless multiply, so AES-GCM costs ~180 ops/round instead of 1-2; (2) unified memory means the GPU shares the CPU's single 120 GB/s memory controller, so offload splits existing bandwidth rather than adding new bandwidth.

METHODOLOGY CAVEAT, IMPORTANT: this machine is on battery with Low Power Mode ENABLED (pmset shows lowpowermode 1). That is why our CPU AES-256-GCM measures 2.85 GB/s single-thread here versus the 5.88 GB/s in results/benchmarks.md - a 2.06x gap. I did not change the setting (system settings are not mine to modify); please re-run with Low Power Mode off and on AC before quoting any absolute number. Two things make the conclusion safe anyway: CPU and GPU were measured under identical conditions so ratios hold, and the numbers that matter most are memory-bound rather than clock-bound - achieved DRAM traffic was 87-94 GB/s against a 120 GB/s spec, i.e. already near full speed. Turning Low Power Mode off will roughly double CPU AES-GCM (toward the ~44 GB/s roofline) while barely moving the memory-bound GPU ChaCha number, so it makes the GPU case strictly WORSE, not better. I also had to control for core type: my first run landed threads on E-cores; the reported numbers use pthread_set_qos_class_self_np(QOS_CLASS_USER_INTERACTIVE) to force P-core placement.

ON QUESTION 6 (does anyone ship this): no production system does bulk symmetric crypto on a GPU. Everything real is research: SSLShader (NSDI 2011, keonjang.github.io/papers/nsdi11ssl.pdf) and AsyncGBP (ICPP 2023). Notably SSLShader's own conclusion is that the GPU win was in RSA (22.6-31.7x, 63K msg/s on a GTX480), not in AES - and its end-to-end result was 13 Gbps = 1.6 GB/s of actual TLS, orders below the kernel-only AES numbers in the same literature. The reasons production skips it are the ones I measured: no GPU AES instruction, latency, and non-parallelizable modes like CBC. Where the industry actually went instead is instructive - dedicated silicon (Intel QuickAssist, NVIDIA BlueField DPUs) and CPU instruction extensions (AES-NI, ARMv8 crypto), both of which beat GPUs per watt. That is the same direction the crate is already going, and pending tasks #7 (8-block AES-GCM pipeline with aggregated GHASH reduction) and #11 (x86-64 AES-NI/PCLMULQDQ) are worth far more than any GPU work.

ONE HONEST CONCESSION: there is a narrow regime where the GPU wins, and it should be stated precisely rather than denied. If ChaCha20-Poly1305 is mandated (AES-GCM disallowed by policy or unavailable), buffers are >= 4 MiB, and >= 200 us of added latency is acceptable, then Metal ChaCha20-Poly1305 at 34-40 GB/s beats even a ring-quality 10-thread NEON CPU implementation (~13 GB/s) by roughly 2.6x. That regime does not describe Blindplane, whose workload is 4 KiB sealed records at 10,233/s - for which the GPU's 120-190 us dispatch floor is 70-110x the CPU's 1.7 us per record.

THE SINGLE CLEANEST ARGUMENT, independent of my implementation quality: constant-time bitsliced AES-256 on the M4 GPU runs at 21.8 GB/s with NO authentication. Our CPU does AES-256-GCM, cipher and GHASH together, at 26.3 GB/s in Low Power Mode. So even granting the GPU a free MAC, it loses. No amount of kernel tuning changes that, because it follows from the GPU lacking an AES instruction.

DEAD ENDS, and why they are dead. (a) T-table AES on GPU, the entire classical literature: measured 10-14.8 GB/s, actually 2x SLOWER than constant-time bitslicing on this hardware because lookups serialize on the LSU - and it is the exact construction broken by Jiang/Fei/Kaeli HPCA 2016 with 10M samples. Rejected twice over. (b) GPU GHASH: 3.86 GB/s, no carryless-multiply instruction on the GPU; would need Shoup tables to go fast, which reintroduces the timing leak. (c) Argon2id on GPU: worth naming explicitly since it is in the crate - do not. Argon2 is deliberately designed so GPUs do it BADLY; that memory-hardness is the entire defence against GPU-equipped password crackers. Making our own Argon2id GPU-friendly would mean weakening the parameter choice that protects users. The GPU is the attacker's tool here and should stay that way. (d) Batching sealed records to amortize dispatch: break-even is 17.4 MB per dispatch (~4,250 records of 4 KiB), which adds >=150 us latency per record and holds thousands of plaintexts in a GPU-visible buffer.

CROSS-CUTTING SECURITY POINT that applies to every GPU path and outweighs the performance discussion: key material and plaintext must live in a MTLBuffer visible to the GPU, the closed-source Apple GPU driver, and its firmware. There is no mlock equivalent, no way to guarantee the driver did not retain a copy, and no reliable way to zeroize - so the crate's secure_erase and Secret types stop meaning what they claim the moment a key crosses into Metal. For a zero-runtime-dependency crate whose pitch is auditability, adding Metal.framework, the Objective-C runtime, a .metallib artifact, an unsafe FFI surface, macOS-only code CI cannot exercise on Linux, and a large closed-source TCB is a steep price for a speedup that is negative for AES and situational for ChaCha.

paths.name: Streaming-SVE (SSVE) ChaCha20 with fused XAR — the actual win in this dimension
paths.hardware: CPU-SME (streaming vector unit, 512-bit SVL), NOT the ZA matrix tiles
paths.algorithms: ChaCha20, XChaCha20 (and the ChaCha half of ChaCha20-Poly1305). Same shape applies to BLAKE2b and Argon2id's G function on .d lanes.
paths.claimed_gain: 4.03x over hand-written NEON on the ChaCha core, measured on this M4. Streaming SVE: 11.50–11.90 GB/s keystream, single P-core. NEON: 2.86–3.03 GB/s.
