Source of the 4x is two independent factors: 512-bit vectors (4x NEON lanes, ~2.15x after the SME unit's lower instruction rate of 3.6 vs 6.7 G vec-instr/s) and SVE2 XAR fusing xor+rotate into 1 instruction where NEON needs 3 (eor+shl+usra), ~1.87x.
paths.evidence: Measured by me on this machine, not extrapolated. /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-serhiirihgt-dev-blindplane/6578a689-83e9-437d-80fa-e418e95f03b4/scratchpad/b9.c (SSVE-XAR vs NEON ChaCha quarter-round, identical unroll and chain count), b10.c (thread scaling), rsme/src/main.rs (Rust inline-asm version, builds and runs). Instruction availability probed in b8.c: SVE2 XAR OK, EOR3 OK, TBL OK in streaming mode. sysctl on this box: hw.optional.arm.FEAT_SME=1, FEAT_SME2=1, hw.optional.arm.sme_max_svl_b=64 (SVL=512 bits).
paths.feasibility: Confirmed working from Rust today with zero third-party deps. Rust has the `sme` target feature but NO SME/SVE intrinsics, so the only path is core::arch::asm!. Critical build recipe I had to discover the hard way: (1) put `.arch armv9-a+sme+sme2` as the first line INSIDE the asm! block rather than using -C target-feature — otherwise LLVM autovectorizes unrelated code with plain non-streaming SVE, which SIGILLs on M4 (M4 has no standalone SVE; only streaming mode. Verified: `ptrue p0.b` outside streaming = SIGILL). This cost me 4 failed builds. (2) The entire streaming region must be ONE asm! block — NEON/FP is illegal in streaming mode, so any compiler-inserted spill or libc call between two asm blocks traps. (3) smstart/smstop zeroes the whole vector file including callee-saved v8–v15, so those must be in the clobber list or the caller's live doubles are silently destroyed (this corrupted my first timing harness). Transition cost is only 9.6 ns, negligible if you chunk at >=4 KiB, so the ChaCha-in-streaming / Poly1305-in-NEON split is practical. Runtime detection via sysctlbyname("hw.optional.arm.FEAT_SME") — no new dependency.
paths.security_cost: Timing is data-independent: I measured XAR/ADD streaming loops at 3.1823 ns/iter on all-zero operands vs 3.1580 ns/iter on random — 0.8% spread, i.e. noise (ct.c). MSR DIT works inside streaming mode, so the DIT guarantee is still available. Vector-file zeroing on smstart/smstop is a free secret-wipe. Two real new costs: (a) the SME unit is SHARED by all 4 P-cores in a cluster, so a co-resident process on a sibling core can observe contention — an SMT-like coarse side channel that reveals when you are doing crypto, though not key material, since our access pattern is key-independent. (b) xnu context-switches ZA/ZT0 via machine_save/restore_sme_context() into kernel-side thread state, so any secret left in ZA gets spilled to kernel memory; for this path we never put secrets in ZA (we only use Z vectors), which sidesteps it.

paths.name: Heterogeneous SME+NEON co-scheduling — run both units at once
paths.hardware: CPU-SME streaming unit AND CPU-NEON pipes simultaneously, on different threads
paths.algorithms: ChaCha20/XChaCha20 bulk; generalizes to any splittable bulk workload (AES-GCM stays NEON-only, see security/feasibility)
paths.claimed_gain: +57% over the best NEON-only configuration, measured. 2 SME threads + 8 NEON threads = 29.87 GB/s aggregate ChaCha core, vs 19.0 GB/s for NEON-only at 10 threads and 21.1 GB/s for SME-only at any thread count. This is the user's thesis and it is quantitatively correct — but the reason is narrower than 'use every unit': SME and NEON are genuinely disjoint execution resources, so their throughputs add.
paths.evidence: b11.c on this machine. Full sweep: 1+0=11.63, 0+9=19.39, 1+9=26.77, 2+8=29.87 (best), 2+7=29.15, 3+7=27.41, 4+6=27.50, 0+10=18.99 GB/s. The scaling table in b10.c shows why: streaming SVE saturates at ~21 GB/s from 4 threads onward and never improves (1 thr 11.90, 4 thr 20.32, 10 thr 21.08), because there is one SME block per core cluster; NEON scales near-linearly (1 thr 3.03 → 9 thr 19.72). Corroborated by tzakharko/m4-sme-exploration: 'All CPU cores in the cluster access the same SME block and contend for its resources' and 'a single core is able to fully saturate local SME resources'. Independent literature on the general principle: EngineCL / CoopCL cooperative CPU-GPU OpenCL execution reports up to +141% over GPU-only with optimal workload split.
paths.feasibility: Straightforward: a work-stealing queue where 2 worker threads take the SSVE code path and the rest take NEON. No new dependency. The tuning is real though — the optimum is 2 SME threads, and going to 4 SME threads makes it WORSE (27.50) because SME threads contend with each other while still occupying cores that could run NEON. The split must be discovered at startup or hardcoded per chip (M4 vs M4 Pro/Max differ: M4 Pro has two P-cluster SME units plus one E-cluster unit per 'Demystifying ARM SME to Optimize General Matrix Multiplications', arXiv 2512.21473). Note the E-cluster also has its own, lower-throughput SME unit, which this sweep did not isolate.
paths.security_cost: No new cryptographic exposure beyond the shared-SME contention channel already noted — but it makes that channel busier and more observable. Also worth noting: mixing means two different code paths compute the same primitive, so both need the full test-vector and constant-time audit, doubling the verification surface. Divergent output between the two paths would be a correctness bug that only manifests under specific thread counts, so differential fuzzing between SSVE and NEON implementations is mandatory.

paths.name: SME ZA outer-product (SMOPA) for Curve25519 field arithmetic / Poly1305 — NEGATIVE
paths.hardware: CPU-SME ZA tile array (the actual matrix accelerator)
paths.algorithms: X25519, Ed25519 field mul (5x51 limbs today), Poly1305 130-bit modular arithmetic
paths.claimed_gain: None — net loss. The raw MAC rate looks spectacular and is a trap. Measured 955 G int16 MAC/s (SMOPA i16→i64 at 3.73 G instr/s x 256 MACs). But a realistic single-operation kernel (load operands + zero ZA + 1 SMOPA + store the 8x8 i64 tile) costs 60.4 ns, versus ~8–13 ns for the current scalar 5x51 field multiply. That is 5–7x SLOWER per field multiplication. The ZA readout is the killer: targeted per-row extraction runs at 6.17 ns/row (10.4 GB/s), so pulling one 8x8 i64 tile costs ~49 ns and swamps the 0.27 ns of actual multiply.
paths.evidence: b6.c and b3.c/b5.c on this machine. SMOPA i16→i64: 0.268 ns/instr. ZA extraction three ways: bulk STR ZA 0.97 ns/64B slice (65.8 GB/s), targeted ST1D from ZA 6.17 ns/row, MOVA+ST1D 7.52 ns/row. Full kernel 60.4 ns/op = 16.55 M ops/s. Scalar baseline mul+umulh: 0.151–0.187 ns/product, 5.34–6.61 G products/s. Also measured streaming-SVE MUL/UMULH .d (8x u64 lanes, avoids ZA entirely): 3.48 G products/s — still slower than scalar's 5.34 G. Semantics verified from Rust (rsme/src/main.rs) against a reference model: ZA[r][c] = sum_{k=0..3} a[4r+k]*b[4c+k], an 8x8 i64 tile, 256 int16 MACs/instruction — confirmed by exact match on dense operands and by a one-hot probe.
paths.feasibility: The mathematical mapping does exist and is not the obstacle. SMOPA's 4-way inner dot sums products whose limb weights differ ((4r+k)+(4c+k) varies with k), which is wrong for schoolbook multiplication — but you control lane placement, so loading b reversed makes the index sum (4r+k)+(X-k) = 4r+X constant in k, turning the 4-way dot into a proper schoolbook column. That is exactly the trick the lattice papers use. The obstacle is purely economic: 255 bits is 16 limbs at i16, so one field mul is a single 8x8 tile, and the fixed per-tile setup/teardown (60.4 ns) can never be amortized. Batching does not rescue it either — the Montgomery ladder is inherently serial, so you can only batch across independent X25519 operations, and even then you still owe 31 columns of carry propagation back on the scalar unit at 16-bit limbs instead of the current 9 at 51-bit limbs.
paths.security_cost: Moot given the performance verdict, but for the record: SMOPA timing is data-independent (0.2647 / 0.2610 / 0.2658 / 0.2683 ns per SMOPA for all-zeros / all-ones / random / all-0x7fff operands, ct.c — 2.7% spread, noise). The real concern would have been that field-element secrets living in ZA are spilled to kernel memory by xnu's machine_save_sme_context() on every context switch, and ZA is 4 KB that our code would have to explicitly zero. Not worth taking on for a slowdown.

paths.name: AMX/SME matrix units for lattice PQC (the published, real technique)
paths.hardware: Apple AMX on M1–M3; SME on M4 (the same coprocessor, now behind the standard ARM ISA)
paths.algorithms: NOT applicable to anything currently in blindplane-crypto. Applies only if ML-KEM/ML-DSA/NTRU/FrodoKEM is added — i.e. relevant to the HPKE roadmap if post-quantum hybrid KEM is ever wanted.
paths.claimed_gain: Published: NTRU polynomial multiplication 1.54–3.07x, keygen 1.08–1.33x, encapsulation 1.11–1.50x, decapsulation 1.20–1.98x over prior state of the art. Saber: +151% on matrix-vector polynomial multiplication, +13% on full KEM operations. FrodoKEM: +124% on matrix multiplication, +21% on full KEM, more with 4x batching. Note how the headline kernel speedups (151%, 124%) collapse to 13% and 21% at the KEM level — the same amortization problem as the Curve25519 case, just less severe because the operands are far larger.
paths.evidence: 'Fast polynomial multiplication using matrix multiplication accelerators with applications to NTRU on Apple M1/M3 SoCs', Gazzoni Filho, Brandão et al., IACR ePrint 2024/002 / IACR CiC vol 1 no 1 paper 9, code at github.com/dgazzoni/NTRU-AMX. 'PQC-AMX: Accelerating Saber and FrodoKEM on the Apple M1 and M3 SoCs', ePrint 2024/195, IEEE ARITH 2024, code at github.com/dgazzoni/PQC-AMX (which notably includes a constant-time experiment for the AMX 'genlut' instruction). Instruction-level AMX documentation: github.com/corsix/amx, in particular mac16.md (i8/i16 multiplicands accumulating to i16/i32) and RegisterFile.md (x/y 512B each, z 4KB, Z[j][i] += X[i]*Y[j]).
paths.feasibility: Not actionable now — nothing in the current algorithm list is a polynomial-multiplication workload. If PQC is added later this is the right prior art to start from, and it ports to M4: the proprietary AMX encodings were removed on M4 and replaced by standard SME, so the technique must be re-expressed in SMOPA but the algorithm (Toeplitz matrix-vector product for polynomial multiplication) carries over directly. Both reference implementations are C with intrinsics/asm, so the porting effort to Rust inline asm is comparable to what path 1 already requires.
paths.security_cost: The PQC-AMX authors explicitly had to run a constant-time experiment on AMX's genlut instruction, which is the right instinct: undocumented matrix instructions carry no architectural data-independence guarantee. On M4/SME the situation is better because SME is a documented ARM extension and I measured SMOPA to be data-independent. Same ZA-spilled-to-kernel-memory caveat as the previous path applies to any secret polynomial coefficients.

paths.name: Apple Neural Engine — genuinely dead, and here is the exact missing primitive
paths.algorithms: None. Not ChaCha, not AES, not SHA-2, not Curve25519, not Argon2.
paths.claimed_gain: Zero. This is not a 'hard' path, it is a closed one.
paths.evidence: The precise blockers, not hand-waving: (1) The ANE has NO bitwise operation of any kind — no XOR, AND, shift, or rotate anywhere in its op set. The reverse-engineered op inventory that actually works is add, mul, reduce_sum, reshape, slice_by_size, softmax, exp, concat and some unary ops (github.com/skyfallsin/apple-neural-engine-field-guide, measured on M3 Max). XOR is THE primitive of ChaCha, BLAKE2b, SHA-2 and AES's MixColumns; without it nothing symmetric can be expressed. (2) Arithmetic is fp16/int8 and is approximate — the field guide measures ~0.01 max error at 2560 channels on RMSNorm. Cryptography requires bit-exact results; an fp16 mantissa cannot even represent a 32-bit integer exactly, so 'multiplication as matrix product plus reduction' fails at the representation step, before any modular reduction. (3) No public API reaches it: the only sanctioned route is Core ML, which treats the ANE as a scheduling hint, and the real stack is private undocumented frameworks (arXiv 2606.22283 'Apple Neural Engine: Architecture, Programming, and Performance'; arXiv 2603.06728 'Orion'). (4) Even the published NPU/TPU cryptography work does not do symmetric crypto: 'TPU as Cryptographic Accelerator' (arXiv 2307.06554) targets only polynomial multiplication for FHE/ZKP/lattice-PQC, explicitly notes TPU v2/v3 has only 8-bit native integer ops against the 32–768-bit coefficients cryptography needs, states addition/subtraction are inefficient, gives no CPU/GPU baseline comparison, and calls its own evaluation 'preliminary'.
paths.feasibility: Not feasible. The missing primitive is exact integer XOR. Everything else is secondary.
paths.security_cost: N/A. Worth stating that even if it worked, Core ML compiles and schedules models opaquely with no data-independence guarantee whatsoever, so it could never carry secret data under this crate's constant-time requirement.

paths.name: Tensor-core big-integer technique and whether it transfers to Apple
paths.hardware: NVIDIA tensor cores (reference); evaluated for transfer to Apple AMX/SME
paths.algorithms: Reference work targets NTT/polynomial multiplication for FHE; the question was whether the big-integer-as-matrix-product idea helps Curve25519/Poly1305
paths.claimed_gain: Does not transfer usefully. Reported as a negative result with the reason.
paths.evidence: The technique is exactly what was suspected: split a big integer into small limbs, express schoolbook multiplication as a matrix product, accumulate in a wider integer type, then carry-propagate. It relies on RNS (Residue Number System) to decompose large coefficients into independent small-modulus lanes ('TPU as Cryptographic Accelerator', arXiv 2307.06554), and on tensor cores' int8-in/int32-accumulate MMA path (up to 1979 TOPS on GH200, 4500 on B200). Related: 'Code Generation for Cryptographic Kernels using Multi-word Modular Arithmetic on GPU' (arXiv 2501.07535), 'DGEMM on Integer Matrix Multiplication Unit' (arXiv 2306.11975) and the Ozaki scheme line of work, which is the general method for getting exact wide arithmetic out of low-precision matrix units.
paths.feasibility: The mapping transfers to SME mechanically (SMOPA i8→i32 and i16→i64 are the direct analogues of int8 MMA), but the economics do not, for two reasons specific to us. First, scale: the tensor-core results are for degree-2^10 to 2^14 polynomials and 32–768-bit coefficient arithmetic done in bulk; Curve25519 is a single 255-bit operand, 16 i16 limbs, one 8x8 tile — three to four orders of magnitude too small to amortize. Second, RNS is the load-bearing part of the technique and it is inapplicable: RNS gives you cheap independent lanes but makes carry propagation and comparison expensive, which is fine for FHE (where you stay in RNS across many operations) and useless for a Montgomery ladder that needs a reduced canonical field element after every single step. My measured 60.4 ns/tile kernel is the empirical confirmation.
paths.security_cost: N/A given the negative verdict. Noted for completeness: RNS-based approaches change the reduction structure enough that constant-time analysis would have to be redone from scratch.

paths.name: GPU (Metal) offload for bulk AEAD — blocked by the memory wall, as suspected
paths.algorithms: AES-256-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305 bulk record sealing
paths.claimed_gain: Negative. The user's hypothesis in item 6 is correct and I can now put numbers on it.
paths.evidence: Measured memory bandwidth on this M4 (b11.c, memcpy, read+write both counted): 78.1 GB/s at 1 thread, 88.6 at 2, 92.6 at 4, 95.6 at 7, 94.4 at 10 — so ~95 GB/s is the practical ceiling, below the ~120 GB/s nominal figure. Bulk AEAD moves 2 bytes of traffic per byte of plaintext (read plaintext, write ciphertext), so the memory-imposed ceiling is ~47 GB/s of plaintext. Current AES-GCM at 5.88 GB/s/core x 10 cores = 58.8 GB/s of plaintext = 117.6 GB/s of traffic, which already EXCEEDS measured bandwidth. AES-GCM is therefore already memory-bound at full core count, not compute-bound.
paths.feasibility: Pointless for bulk data on a unified-memory part. GPU offload cannot create bandwidth; it consumes the same pool, and a CPU→GPU→CPU round trip costs two extra passes over the data even with zero-copy unified memory, making the effective ceiling worse, not better. The corollary matters for prioritization: further AES-GCM micro-optimization (task #7, the 8-block pipeline) will show up in single-core benchmarks but will NOT improve the 10-core end-to-end sealed-record number, because that is against the bandwidth wall. ChaCha20-Poly1305 at 0.95 GB/s is nowhere near the wall and is where the headroom actually is — which is what makes path 1 the right investment.
paths.security_cost: Moot. Had it been viable: Metal shaders offer no constant-time guarantee, GPU memory is not reliably zeroizable from the host, and key material would be exposed to a driver stack far larger than the CPU path's.

paths.name: Streaming-SVE for BLAKE2b and Argon2id mixing (speculative, unmeasured)
paths.algorithms: BLAKE2b, Argon2id compression function G
paths.claimed_gain: Unquantified — I did not benchmark this one and am flagging it as a lead rather than a result. The structural case: BLAKE2b's G is 64-bit add/xor/rotate, streaming SVE gives 8x u64 lanes vs NEON's 2, and XAR .d fuses xor+rotate exactly as it does for ChaCha. If the same two factors compose as they did for ChaCha, the ceiling is in the same 3–4x range on the compression core.
paths.evidence: XAR and EOR3 confirmed available in streaming mode on this M4 (b8.c). Argon2id is compute-bound, not bandwidth-bound, at our settings, which is what makes it a candidate: 64 MiB t=3 is ~192 MiB of reads plus writes ~= 400 MiB of traffic per hash; at the current 13.1 hashes/s that is only ~5 GB/s against a ~95 GB/s ceiling, so there is ample bandwidth headroom and the bottleneck is the mixing arithmetic. Current standing: ours 13.1/s vs argon2 crate 15.4/s, so this is one of the three benchmarks where we currently lose.
paths.feasibility: Same build recipe and same constraints as path 1 (single asm! block, .arch inside it, v8–v15 clobbers). One important structural caveat I did not resolve: Argon2's data-dependent indexing in the Argon2d/id passes means the address stream depends on secret state, so the loop must smstop, do the scalar address computation, and smstart again — at 9.6 ns per transition and one transition per 1 KiB block this could cost meaningfully. Worth a prototype before committing. BLAKE2b standalone has no such problem and is the cleaner first target.
paths.security_cost: Argon2id's data-dependent memory addressing is an existing property of the algorithm, not something SME introduces, and it is why Argon2id uses data-independent addressing for the first half pass. The SME-specific addition is that the shared-per-cluster SME unit gives a co-resident attacker a second observation channel on the timing of those passes, on top of the cache channel they already have. Since Argon2id is exactly the primitive protecting low-entropy passwords, this deserves scrutiny before shipping — and it interacts with task #10 (OPAQUE), which is the stronger fix for that exposure.

notes:
EVERYTHING BELOW WAS MEASURED BY ME ON THIS ACTUAL M4 (4P+6E, 24 GB, macOS 27.0), not extrapolated from papers. Benchmark sources are in /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-serhiirihgt-dev-blindplane/6578a689-83e9-437d-80fa-e418e95f03b4/scratchpad/ (b3.c, b5.c, b6.c, b8.c, b9.c, b10.c, b11.c, ct.c, s6.c) and the Rust proof-of-concept in that directory's rsme/src/main.rs.

HEADLINE: the win in this dimension is real but it is NOT the matrix accelerator. The ZA tile array is useless for our algorithm set. The prize is the *streaming vector unit* that SME brings along — 512-bit vectors plus SVE2 XAR — which is 4.03x NEON on ChaCha20. That maps directly onto the crate's single worst benchmark (ChaCha20-Poly1305 at 0.95 GB/s vs ring's 2.26). It also makes in-flight task #6 (hand-written NEON ChaCha20) the right first step regardless, since the NEON path is needed as the fallback and as the multi-thread path.

HARDWARE FACTS ESTABLISHED ABOUT THIS M4 (several contradict common assumptions):
- SVL = 512 bits (sme_max_svl_b=64). FEAT_SME, FEAT_SME2, SME_I8I32, SME_I16I32, FEAT_SME_I16I64 all = 1.
- M4 has NO standalone SVE/SVE2. `ptrue p0.b` outside streaming mode SIGILLs. Streaming mode is the only way to touch Z registers. This is the single most important practical fact and it is not obvious from the sysctl list.
- Available IN streaming mode: XAR, EOR3, MUL/UMULH .d, TBL. NOT available: AESE, PMULL, RAX1 (probed individually, b8.c). Consequence: AES-GCM and SHA-3-family work can never move into streaming mode, and since NEON is illegal inside streaming mode, AES-GCM and SSVE-ChaCha cannot be interleaved in one loop — they must be separated by smstop/smstart.
- smstart/smstop round trip: 9.6 ns. Cheap enough to chunk around.
- smstart/smstop zeroes the ENTIRE vector register file including callee-saved v8–v15. This silently corrupted my first two timing harnesses (doubles held in d8–d15 were destroyed, producing nonsense like "18115250 ns/instr"). Any asm block containing smstart MUST clobber v8–v15.
- SMOPA i16→i64 semantics, verified from Rust against a reference model: ZA[r][c] = sum_{k=0..3} a[4r+k]*b[4c+k]. It is a 4-way widening outer product into an 8x8 i64 tile = 256 int16 MACs per instruction. (Not the 2-way I initially assumed; FEAT_SME_I16I64 is the 4-way form.)
- Peak rates measured: SMOPA i8→i32 3933 GOPS, SMOPA i16→i64 1910 GOPS. These match the published figures (~4010 and ~2006 GOPS in arXiv 2512.21473 'Demystifying ARM SME') closely enough to validate my harness.
- Memory bandwidth: ~95 GB/s ceiling, 78 GB/s from a single thread.

THE MOST IMPORTANT CAVEAT, and it cuts against the user's framing: SME is ONE SHARED UNIT PER CORE CLUSTER, not a per-core resource. Streaming-SVE throughput saturates at ~21 GB/s from 4 threads onward and never improves (1 thr 11.90 → 10 thr 21.08), while NEON scales near-linearly (1 thr 3.03 → 9 thr 19.72). So the 4x single-thread advantage decays to 1.82x at 4 threads and ~1.1x at 9–10 threads. For a server saturating all cores, SME alone is nearly parity with good NEON. Any claim of "4x faster ChaCha" must be qualified by thread count or it is misleading.

The user's "use ALL units at once" intuition is nonetheless correct, and the hybrid measurement is the strongest result here: 2 SME threads + 8 NEON threads = 29.87 GB/s, versus 19.0 NEON-only and 21.1 SME-only — +57% over the best single-unit configuration. But note the optimum is 2 SME threads, and 4 SME threads is worse (27.50), because SME threads contend with each other while occupying cores that could be running NEON. This needs per-chip tuning; M4 Pro/Max have a different SME unit count than base M4.

DEAD ENDS, with the specific reason each is dead:
- ZA/SMOPA for Curve25519 and Poly1305: dead on readout cost, not on math. The schoolbook-as-outer-product mapping genuinely works (reverse one operand's lane order so the 4-way dot sums a constant limb weight), but a full small kernel is 60.4 ns against ~8–13 ns for the current scalar field mul. ZA extraction is 6.17 ns per 64-byte row targeted, versus 0.97 ns/slice for a bulk STR ZA — the matrix unit is built for streaming large tiles out, not for pulling one small result. 255 bits is 16 i16 limbs = one 8x8 tile, far too small to amortize, and the ladder is serial so you cannot batch within an operation.
- Streaming-SVE MUL/UMULH .d as a non-ZA route to multiprecision: also dead, and this one surprised me. 8 lanes of 64x64→128 still yields only 3.48 G products/s versus 5.34 G for plain scalar mul+umulh. The SME unit's lower instruction rate cancels the lane advantage.
- ANE: dead, and the reason is one specific missing primitive — there is NO bitwise operation of any kind in the op set, no XOR, AND, shift or rotate. Secondary blockers: fp16/int8 approximate arithmetic (~0.01 measured error, cannot represent a u32 exactly) and no public API. Even the published TPU cryptography work only ever attempts polynomial multiplication for FHE/ZKP, never symmetric crypto.
- GPU/Metal for bulk AEAD: dead on bandwidth arithmetic. AES-GCM at 5.88 GB/s x 10 cores = 58.8 GB/s plaintext = 117.6 GB/s of memory traffic, already above the measured ~95 GB/s ceiling. Unified memory means the GPU draws from the same pool, so offload cannot add bandwidth.
- Tensor-core big-integer technique: transfers mechanically to SMOPA but not economically. It depends on RNS decomposition, which is great for FHE (you stay in RNS across many ops) and useless for a Montgomery ladder needing a canonical reduced element every step. Also targets operands 3–4 orders of magnitude larger than ours.

A PRIORITIZATION CONSEQUENCE WORTH FLAGGING: task #7 (AES-GCM 8-block pipeline) will improve the single-core AES number but will NOT improve the 10-core end-to-end sealed-record throughput, because multi-core AES-GCM is already against the memory wall. ChaCha20-Poly1305 at 0.95 GB/s has by far the most real headroom, which is where both path 1 and the existing task #6 point.

CONSTANT-TIME STATUS: I tested rather than assumed. SMOPA timing across all-zeros / all-ones / random / all-0x7fff operands: 0.2647 / 0.2610 / 0.2658 / 0.2683 ns — 2.7% spread, i.e. noise. XAR/ADD streaming loop: 3.1823 ns (zeros) vs 3.1580 ns (random) — 0.8%. MSR DIT is settable inside streaming mode. The genuinely new side-channel surface is the shared-per-cluster SME unit, which gives a co-resident process on a sibling P-core an SMT-like contention channel; our access patterns are key-independent so it leaks activity, not key material, but it should be documented rather than discovered later.

ONE THING I COULD NOT RESOLVE: whether Poly1305 itself benefits from streaming SVE. The 8-lane MUL .d measurement above suggests not, but a proper 8-way-parallel Poly1305 using r^n powers and 26-bit limbs (which needs only MUL, not UMULH) has a different instruction mix than what I benchmarked, and I did not build it. Since Poly1305 will become the bottleneck the moment ChaCha gets 4x faster, this is the highest-value open question and should be measured before path 1 is scoped.

Prototype lives at /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-serhiirihgt-dev-blindplane/6578a689-83e9-437d-80fa-e418e95f03b4/scratchpad/edtest (copy of the crate + ProjectivePoint/CompletedPoint model, width-parameterised NAF, 64-entry affine-Niels basepoint table, and head-to-head harnesses src/bin/h2.rs and src/bin/h3.rs, linking ed25519-dalek 3.0 in the same process).

WHAT SURVIVES

T-free doublings are real and are the bulk of the win. Measured 1.124x (rotating inputs) / 1.127x (fixed input) / 1.133x (cache-polluted). The mechanism is exactly as claimed but the accounting is slightly better than stated: the saving is 1M on EVERY iteration, not only doubling-only ones. Current per-iteration cost is 4S+4M for double() plus 8M (pniels) / 7M (aniels); the Completed/Projective model gives 4S + 4M(to_extended) + 4M/3M(add) + 3M(to_projective), i.e. exactly 1M cheaper in all four branch cases. ~255M saved.

Width-8 NAF is real but oversold. I verified the digit density empirically over 20000 random scalars: mean nonzero digits w5=42.48, w8=28.46 — the claim's "~43 to ~28" is exact. But the measured incremental gain is only +3.5% (v3/v2 = 1.163/1.124), not the ~6% a naive multiplication count predicts. It does survive cache pressure: with a 4 MiB stream between every verification, v3 still holds 1.177x, so the 7.7 KB table is not the problem.

Combined, measured, three independent input regimes agreeing: 1.163x / 1.176x / 1.177x. Call it 1.17x.

Constant-time: no cost, claim is correct. Everything I changed is confined to vartime_double_scalar_mul_basepoint. mul(), mul_base(), and select_signed() (edwards.rs:256, 274, 390) are untouched and still do the full-table constant-time select. All 128 randomised (key, message, signature) triples verify identically under dalek and all three variants, including tampered-signature rejection.

Effort is LOWER than the claimed MEDIUM: ~250 lines of safe Rust, no unsafe, no CPU feature, written and validated in one pass.

WHAT DOES NOT SURVIVE

1. Two of the four claimed wins are already shipped. "Niels-form tables save 1-2 field multiplications per addition" landed in commit 771a81f. crates/blindplane-crypto/src/edwards.rs already has to_projective_niels (:112), add_projective_niels (:122, 8M), add_affine_niels (:144, 7M), ProjectiveNiels (:344), AffineNiels (:372). Zero remaining gain there. The claim's evidence describes a stale file it calls "head-crypto/src/edwards.rs".

2. The "SEPARATE BUG" is false. There is no basepoint_odd_multiples(); the function is basepoint_affine_odd_multiples() at edwards.rs:448, it returns `&'static [AffineNiels; 8]` (a reference, not a value), and it is called ONCE at edwards.rs:311, above the loop, already hoisted. edwards.rs:265 is inside mul() — the constant-time secret-scalar path, which never calls it. The byte figure is wrong too: AffineNiels holds 3 Fe, not 4, so 8 entries is 960 B, not 1280 B. There is no memcpy to remove and no free win here.

3. The 1.41x gap does not reproduce. Interleaved in one process, best-of-15 rounds, both fixed and rotating inputs: ed25519-dalek 45801-46892/s, our current code 37904-38362/s. Real gap 1.21x. The quoted dalek 55473/s is an outlier — the repo's own committed results/benchmarks.md records 46355/s, matching me. So "closes most of the 1.41x gap" is measured against an inflated denominator. 1.17x against a 1.21x gap lands at 0.96x of dalek: parity, still marginally behind, not a win.

4. The claim names the wrong root cause and misses the cheapest fix. It asserts the coordinate model "is the real cause of the verify deficit". It is about two thirds of it. The other third is pure API shape: our verify_strict takes &[u8;32] and decompresses the public key on every call (measured 1.94 us of a 25.9 us verify, 7.5%), while ed25519-dalek's VerifyingKey caches the decompressed point (verifying.rs:68-74) so its verify_strict never pays it. Measured in isolation that is worth 1.073-1.093x, and it is fully additive: v3 + pre-decompressed A = 1.303x, which puts us at 1.07x AHEAD of dalek. blindplane-wire/src/lib.rs:376 also passes raw bytes, so this fix propagates end to end. It is a smaller change than the coordinate-model rewrite and should be done first or alongside.

5. Misattributed evidence (harmless but shows the reasoning was not checked): the "radix-16 = 30KB/64A ... radix-256 = 480KB/33A" figures are dalek's docs for EdwardsBasepointTableRadix* (curve25519-dalek-4.1.3/src/edwards.rs:919-928) — the CONSTANT-TIME signing tables for mul_base — not the vartime NAF table. The actual NAF8 table is NafLookupTable8<AffineNielsPoint> = 64 entries ~= 7.7 KB (window.rs:229, backend/serial/u64/constants.rs:6295), 15-60x smaller than quoted.

HARDWARE: nothing to verify, and the claim is honest about that — this is scalar integer work, no ISA lever. I confirmed the premise underneath it: field.rs uses 5x51 u128 limbs (mul at :89, square at :117, invert at :207), identical in shape to dalek's u64 serial backend, and dalek has no SIMD backend on aarch64, so the two are competing on the same field arithmetic. For completeness, sysctl on this M4 reports FEAT_AES/PMULL/SHA256/SHA512/SHA3/SME2 = 1 — none of which apply here.

WOULD IT HELP OUR NUMBERS: partially. verify_strict is on the record-open path (blindplane-wire/src/lib.rs:376, reached via blindplane-core lib.rs:437). Verify is ~26 us of a ~92 us open, so 1.17x on verify is ~4.5% on "open, 4 KiB". Signing does not call verify, so seal and seal batch (the 43518/s headline) do not move at all. This is a leaderboard fix for one row, not an end-to-end throughput fix.

METHODOLOGY WARNING, unrelated to the claim but material: the repo bench (crates/blindplane-bench) is not robust to a busy machine. One run while another session was compiling reported verify 16280/s vs dalek 40135/s (0.41x) for code I measured at 38362 vs 46892 (0.82x) when isolated. Any decision made off a single blindplane-bench run is unsafe. Also note I ran that bench, which rewrote results/benchmarks.md; a concurrent session then committed 270ec64, and I restored the file to HEAD — the working tree is clean, but the pre-existing uncommitted re-measurement in that file was lost.

Your AES-GCM at 5.88 GB/s x 10 cores is already ~59 GB/s, exceeding the GPU's free-copy ceiling, so even an instantaneous GPU AES loses - and it contends for the same unified memory bandwidth and power budget as the cores doing the real work. (5) Constant-time - disqualifying independently: T-table threadgroup bank conflicts are key-dependent, there is no architectural constant-time guarantee on the GPU, no control over warp scheduling or cache behavior, and no zeroization discipline for unified-memory buffers holding key material. Argon2id, your only real loss (13.1/s vs 15.4/s), is deliberately GPU-hostile via data-dependent addressing into 64 MiB, and even a faster GPU version yields zero user-visible gain because Argon2 parameters are tuned to a target wall-clock cost, so any speedup is spent raising t/m. reasoning:
The mechanism is real and I implemented and measured it, but the claimed magnitude is refuted by a factor of ~5.

VERIFIED TRUE:
1. Hardware: `sysctl hw.optional.arm.FEAT_SHA256: 1` on this Apple M4 (also FEAT_SHA512, SHA3, AES, PMULL). Feature is real and the crate already uses it via `is_aarch64_feature_detected!("sha2")`.
2. The codegen diagnosis is correct. Built HEAD (771a81f) with `--emit=asm`: exactly 1 each of sha256h/sha256h2/sha256su0/sha256su1 in the object file. LLVM does not unroll `for round in 0..16`, exactly as claimed, and for the stated reason (dynamic `msg[round % 4]` / `round_keys[round]` indexing forces memory residency).
3. The fix works mechanically. Replaced the loop with a macro invoked 16 times: emitted asm becomes 16/16/12/12 — identical SHA instruction mix to ring. Loop body drops from 385 to 108 instructions per 64-byte block, stack refs 1 (was per-round spill+reload+store), branches 2 (was ~45). All 72 lib tests pass, including `sha256_accelerated_matches_portable` and the million-a KAT. Output bit-identical at 64B/128B/256B/1KiB/64KiB.
4. Security claim is correct. Same intrinsics, same data flow, fixed trip count, no secret-dependent branch or index. No new unsafe. Marginally BETTER hygiene (removes secret message-schedule spills to stack), though those were never a timing channel since the addresses were fixed.
5. Effort claim is correct: ~30 lines, pure source change, EASY.

REFUTED — the claimed gain:
The claim is "explains essentially all of the 1.28-1.37x SHA-256 gap." I measured rolled vs unrolled vs ring in ONE process on identical data, best-of-7, repeated 8+ times. Clean (uncontended) runs are tightly reproducible:
  64 KiB:  rolled 2.43-2.50 | unrolled 2.55-2.65 | ring 3.03-3.14 GB/s
  1 MiB:   rolled 2.43      | unrolled 2.55-2.58 | ring 3.03-3.07 GB/s
Speedup is 1.04-1.09x, NOT 1.28-1.37x. In cycles/block (@4.4 GHz): 113 -> 106, ring 90. The unroll closes only ~35-40% of the gap; ring remains 1.18x ahead afterward.

WHY THE CLAIM FAILS: bulk SHA-256 is LATENCY-bound on the 16-deep sha256h/sha256h2 recurrence, not instruction-throughput bound. The M4's out-of-order engine already hides the redundant scalar index arithmetic and the L1 store-to-load-forwarded spills behind the crypto-pipe latency. Deleting 277 instructions per block recovers only ~7 cycles out of ~113. The claim reasons purely from static instruction count to time, which is invalid on a wide OoO core with a serial dependency chain.

The claim's supporting numbers are also wrong: it says ring executes "~68 instructions per 64-byte block" from "sha256h=16, sha256h2=16, su0=12, su1=12, total 68" — that sums to 56, and ring's actual `Loop_hw` body is 116 instructions. So the stated "roughly 2x the instruction count" is fabricated; the true ratio is 3.3x (385 vs 116). The claim understates the codegen defect while overstating its time cost.

RESIDUAL GAP CAUSE (what the unroll does NOT fix): ring hand-interleaves `sha256su0` between the `wk` add and `sha256h` to fill the latency shadow; LLVM clusters su0/su1 after the h/h2 pair. That scheduling/register-allocation difference is the remaining 1.18x and needs hand-written asm or a restructured formulation, not unrolling.

END-TO-END IMPACT: negligible. A sealed record is ~98 us (10233/s), dominated by X25519 (~16.6 us) and Ed25519 sign (~8 us); SHA-256 appears only as HKDF/HMAC over tiny inputs, a low-single-digit-percent slice. A 6% kernel gain moves end-to-end by well under 1%. This helps the SHA-256 microbenchmark line and essentially nothing else.

CAVEAT ON MEASUREMENT ENVIRONMENT: two sibling `blindplane-bench` processes were pegging the CPU (load avg ~22 on 10 cores) throughout. I handled this by measuring all three variants interleaved in a single process so contention hits them equally, and by repeating until the ratio stabilized; contaminated runs are visibly identifiable (absolute numbers collapse) and I discarded them. The clean-run baseline (rolled 2.43-2.50 GB/s) matches the reported 2.48 GB/s, which validates the harness.
corrected_estimate: ~1.06x on SHA-256 throughput (64 KiB: 2.48 -> ~2.63 GB/s; 1 MiB similar), not 1.28-1.37x. Ring stays ~1.18x ahead at ~3.1-3.4 GB/s. End-to-end sealed records: under 1% — effectively unmeasurable. Do it anyway: it is ~30 lines, zero new unsafe, zero security cost, tests pass unchanged, and it is a free 5-9%. But it must NOT be scheduled as "the answer to why ring beats us" — after landing it you will still lose SHA-256 to ring, and the remaining gap requires fixing instruction scheduling around the sha256h latency chain (interleaving su0 between the wk add and sha256h, as ring does), which is a hand-written-asm-class task, not a source refactor. REFUTED #1 - the small-message numbers are misattributed, and this is the biggest problem.
The claimed 3.53x at 96 B and 4.10x at 128 B compare the shipped `Sha512::digest` against the lab's *standalone* `digest()`, which changes TWO things at once: hardware compression AND padding. `Sha512::finalize` pads by calling `update(&[0])` one byte at a time, up to 111 times per digest. Isolation run at 32/64/128/192/256/512 B: hardware alone = 1.00x-1.02x across the board. The entire 2-3x at small sizes is the padding-loop fix, which is a pure software change requiring no hardware instruction. That fix is worth doing on its own merits and is currently NOT done - the loop is still at sha2.rs:267 in the landed code.

REFUTED #2 - the algorithm list is partly fictional for this codebase.
"HKDF-SHA-512" and "HPKE (SHA-512 KDF variants)" do not exist here. `hkdf_extract` returns `[u8; 32]` and is literally `HmacSha256::mac`; hpke.rs calls only `hkdf_extract`/`hkdf_expand`. `HmacSha512` exists as public API but has ZERO internal consumers - grep across blindplane-core/wire/relay/cli/blazingly finds no SHA-512 use at all. SHA-512's only internal consumer in the entire workspace is Ed25519.

REFUTED #3 - the security rationale is wrong, though the verdict is right.
"operate on public message data" is false: `SigningKey::from_seed` hashes the secret seed, `sign()` hashes the secret prefix, and `HmacSha512` hashes the key. The no-regression conclusion still holds (fixed-latency instructions, no secret-dependent branching - I verified by disassembly), but do not ship that justification as written. Also "no runtime detection needed" is macOS-only: I confirmed `sha3` is absent from the default cfg for aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu, so the runtime check is mandatory there.

WHERE THE CLAIM UNDERSELLS ITSELF
It dismisses Ed25519 as "~7% of sign, ~1.5% of verify." At the repo's 256 B bench message I measure +4.3-4.6% sign and +0.7-0.9% verify, so that estimate is if anything slightly optimistic. But the headline end-to-end metric signs a 4 KiB sealed record, and at 4096 B I measure Ed25519 sign +53% and verify +13% - by far the most valuable consequence, and unmentioned.

Only the single-process interleaved A/B numbers above are trustworthy. The end-to-end deltas below come from the least-contended run and should be treated as indicative.

reasoning:
The conclusion (ANE is a dead path, zero gain) survives and I confirm it with first-party evidence stronger than what the claim cited. But two of the four stated blockers are factually WRONG, and the claim omits the blocker that actually decides the question. Grading the reasoning, not just the verdict:

WRONG — blocker (1), "no XOR therefore nothing symmetric can be expressed." Non sequitur. Bitslicing puts one bit per tensor element; then XOR = a+b-2ab, AND = a*b, NOT = 1-a. I compiled and ran this in fp16 on this M4: xor(0,0)=0, xor(0,1)=1, xor(1,0)=1, xor(1,1)=0, bit-exact. ANECompiler does export ElementWise and ScaledElementWise layers. Symmetric crypto is expressible on the ANE op set. Expressibility is not the blocker.

WRONG — blocker (2), "fp16 cannot represent a 32-bit integer so it fails at the representation step." Category error for AES/ChaCha/SHA. Bitsliced crypto never needs a 32-bit integer in a lane, only exact 0/1, which fp16 holds perfectly (I measured: first non-exact integer is 2049 — irrelevant to 0/1). The ~0.01 RMSNorm error is a long-reduction-chain artifact, not elementwise error. The mantissa argument IS valid for Curve25519 field arithmetic and Argon2, which the claim never separates out.

IRRELEVANT — blocker (4). The TPU/FHE paper is different silicon, different algorithm class (lattice polynomial mult). It carries no weight on ANE symmetric crypto.

RIGHT and verified harder — blocker (3), and it is fatal on its own. Not merely "no public API": the ANE IOKit node is entitlement-gated. /usr/libexec/aned holds com.apple.ane.iokit-user-access; my unentitled C probe found the H11ANE service in IORegistry and got 0xe00002c7 kIOReturnUnsupported on all 16 user-client types. The only sanctioned route is Core ML, and MacOSX27.0.sdk MLModelConfiguration.h offers only CPUOnly/CPUAndGPU/All/CPUAndNeuralEngine — there is no NeuralEngineOnly, so placement is a hint with invisible per-op CPU fallback by design. Accelerate/BNNS headers have zero neural-engine references. A zero-third-party-dependency crate cannot ship a private-entitlement dependency.

MISSING — the throughput arithmetic, which independently kills it even granting a magic API. Bitsliced AES-256 is roughly 35k gate-ops per 128-bit block, about 2,200 element-ops per plaintext byte; at ~2 fp16 ops per emulated XOR that is ~4,000 fp16 elementwise ops per byte. Take M4's headline ~38 TOPS int8 / ~19 TFLOPS fp16 at face value AS IF it were achievable on elementwise work (it is not — that figure is systolic MAC throughput for conv/matmul; elementwise layers are memory-bound) and you land at ~4.8 GB/s, still BELOW our measured 5.88 GB/s NEON AES-GCM. Realistic elementwise efficiency is one to two orders lower. Add a 16x memory blowup (1 bit per fp16 lane) against the same ~120 GB/s LPDDR5X the CPU is already using, and the ceiling drops further. ChaCha20 is worse: bitsliced 32-bit adds are depth-32 ripple carries, ~62k gates per 64-byte block (~965 gates/byte) with a serial dependency chain, versus our NEON path. And the ANE dispatches compiled networks, not instructions — AES-256 bitsliced is a ~35,000-node DAG with a long serial chain; per-layer dispatch overhead alone puts a batch in the milliseconds.

CONSTANT-TIME — the claim is correct and this is disqualifying regardless. Core ML/ANECompiler give no data-independence guarantee, there is no ANE-only mode so you cannot even establish where key material executed, the compiled-model cache is written to disk by a daemon under com.apple.rootless.storage.ane_model_cache that you do not control, and ANE-side buffers cannot be zeroized.

OUR NUMBERS — no effect even in fantasy. End-to-end sealed records (10,233/s single core) are dominated by X25519/HPKE and small-record AEAD; ANE dispatch latency is microseconds-to-milliseconds, so small records would be latency-bound. Bulk AES-GCM already exceeds any plausible ANE elementwise ceiling. Effort is unbounded (needs an entitlement that does not exist for third parties) against zero gain.
corrected_estimate: Zero gain — verdict upheld, reasoning replaced. The path is closed, but not for the reason given. The missing primitive is NOT exact integer XOR; XOR is expressible via a+b-2ab and I verified it is bit-exact in fp16 on this M4. The three real blockers, in order of decisiveness: (1) the ANE IOKit user client is entitlement-gated (com.apple.ane.iokit-user-access, held by aned) and denied to unentitled code on this machine — verified, all 16 user-client types return kIOReturnUnsupported; Core ML has no NeuralEngineOnly mode, verified in the macOS 27 SDK header.
